opts.t: "ALIVE STOP TELL ME ABOUT THE COAL MAN STOP"

say.t: HA STOP KNEW YOU WERE A GOSSIP UNDERNEATH STOP
LIAR STOP NOBODY IS BUSY AT A RELAY SHACK STOP

opts.t: Tap back a single dot. Received.

say.t: A DOT STOP YOU ARE IMPOSSIBLE STOP

lines.t: I didn't talk much. I never have. But she didn't seem to mind. She talked enough for two.

scenes.goal: Take up your new post at the relay shack

lines.t: Toby rides out to the shack, which nobody ever does. He's got his serious face on.

It's Rosie. Her sweetheart, the one from the photograph — they're finished. It was bad, Eli. She telephoned me in the middle of the night. She was... in a very dark place. She said things that scared me.
Is she alright?
She is now. She's got people. Her sister's with her. I just thought you'd want to know.
Something terrible and hopeful happens in Eli's chest at the same time.
I hated that I felt it. She was hurting, and some small selfish part of me thought: now she won't love anyone else. Now maybe...

choice.prompt: Toby is watching you.

opts.t: "I hope she's alright. Truly. That's what matters."

say.t: Yeah. It is.

opts.t: "Do you think she'd want to hear from me?"

say.t: I don't know. Wait a while. Her birthday's in a month. Wish her well. Just that.

lines.t: A month later, on her birthday, he sends a short, careful wire. HAPPY BIRTHDAY STOP HOPE THE YEAR IS KIND TO YOU STOP. She wires back: THANK YOU STOP.
Two words. He reads them all evening.

scenes.goal: Toby has ridden all the way out to see you

lines.t: Then, out of nowhere, a message on the Port Ellis line addressed to the relay shack. To him.
ELI STOP NEED HELP WITH A PAPER ON ROENTGEN WIRING STOP YOU KNOW WIRES STOP ARE YOU BUSY STOP
He is never busy. He helps. They wire back and forth for two weeks. Coils and currents, and then jokes about her professor, and then how her mother is, and how his is.
YOU WERE ALWAYS CLEVER STOP I REMEMBER THE WINDOW SEAT STOP

choice.prompt: It feels like being friends. Real friends, finally.

opts.t: Enjoy it. Ask for nothing more.

say.t: For two weeks, it was like we were fifteen on that porch again. Except we were talking.

opts.t: Bring up the past. Just a little.

say.t: DO YOU REMEMBER THE PILLARS STOP
A long pause on the line. Then: PAPER IS DUE FRIDAY STOP. You don't bring it up again.

opts.t: Help with the paper and nothing else.

scenes.goal: Answer the wire from Port Ellis

lines.t: September. Her birthday again. He wires good wishes and asks how the paper turned out.
The wire company sends back a slip: DELIVERED. RECEIVED. No reply.
Then he and Ezra plan a trip north, to the Dakota hills. She's working at a hospital near there now. He wires to ask if she knows a good boarding house in that town.
DELIVERED. RECEIVED. No reply.
She saw it. She just didn't answer.
Maybe she's busy.
Eli.
...I know.
Left on "received." There's a special kind of quiet in that word.

notices: The Dakota hills, blue at dawn
A town you'll never see again

choice.prompt: On the trip, Ezra asks if you're alright.

say.t: Me too. Even though you snore.
You've been saying that since the seventh year. It's never once been true.

scenes.goal: Meet Ezra at the depot for your trip north

lines.t: He tries the Lonely Hearts column in the Ironwood paper. Once. Rook dares him, and he's too tired to argue.
Two replies for box 14, Mr. Ashby.

The first is from a schoolteacher up north. They write five letters. She's funny and careful. Then her letters simply stop, mid-conversation, like a door left open on an empty room. He writes twice more and gives up.
The second is from a woman in Red Bluff who, by her third letter, mentions her husband.
Why do married women write to the Lonely Hearts? Why does anybody write to anybody and then vanish? I'm so tired of being the one left holding the pen.

choice.prompt: The clerk is waiting.

opts.t: Laugh about it. "Well. At least I tried."

say.t: That's the spirit, Mr. Ashby.

scenes.goal: Collect replies to your notice in the Lonely Hearts column

lines.t: Since the new year, he's had a feeling. A cold, heavy feeling, like weather coming. Something bad is on its way. He couldn't say what.
Sit down. Have you heard?
Heard what?
I didn't want you reading it in the paper. There's a rumor. About Rosie. That she's getting married.
Eli laughs, actually laughs.
That's not true. She'd— that's not true.
I hope it isn't. I'm just telling you what I heard.

choice.prompt: Rook's hand is on your arm.

say.t: Brother from another mother. Who else was going to?

scenes.goal: Meet Rook at the Kettle & Lamp

lines.t: The eighteenth of January. It's in the Port Ellis Herald. The engagement notice.

card.title: The Port Ellis Herald
card.body: Dr. and Mrs. H. Marlowe announce the engagement of their daughter, Miss Rosalind Marlowe, to Dr. A. Pemberton of the Royal Infirmary, Liverpool. The couple will make their home abroad.

lines.t: Not the sweetheart from the photograph. Not anyone she loved. An arranged match, the gossip says. A doctor of her parents' choosing, older than her, same church, a position overseas.
I'd have done anything. Changed churches. Crossed an ocean. Become a doctor, if that's what it took. I'm not stupid. I could have done it. I just never thought I'd have to.
And she didn't even marry someone she loved. She married someone she was handed.
He walks to the key at the back of the office. The clerk is at lunch. He puts his hand on the brass and taps.
WHY STOP WHY STOP WHY WOULD YOU STOP EVERYONE CHANGES THEIR MIND STOP STUPID STOP STUPID PEOPLE STOP I COULD HAVE STOP I COULD HAVE STOP
XXXXXX EEEEE TTTTTTTTTTTTT 9999 STOP STOP STOP STOP
The line isn't connected to anything. It goes nowhere. He taps until his fingers ache.

choice.prompt: The clerk comes back. You take your hand off the key.

say.t: You alright, Mr. Ashby?
No. But I will be. I think.

opts.t: Sit down on the floor behind the counter.

say.t: The clerk doesn't say anything. He puts a cup of water next to you, and goes back to sorting the mail.

lines.t: It felt like watching someone I loved die right in front of me. And I couldn't do anything. And I wasn't allowed to grieve, because she wasn't mine to lose.

scenes.goal: Read the Port Ellis paper at the post office

lines.t: She starts appearing in his dreams. Every night. Sometimes she's fifteen, on the porch. Sometimes she's a stranger in a wedding dress who doesn't know him.
He wakes with his heart going too fast and his hands shaking. It happens in the day too. At the key. On the coach. His hands just... shake.
Then a wire from Mr. Hargrove: the relay shack is closing. Everybody back to the main office by the middle of February. Two to ten, every day.
You're not sleeping.
I'm sleeping.
I hear you walking. Every night. Up and down. Like your Pa used to before a long ride.

choice.prompt: Ma has her hand on the door.

opts.t: "Something's wrong with me, Ma. I don't know what."

say.t: Then we'll find out what. That's all. You don't have to know yet. You just have to not hide it.
It's not work. But I'll wait till you're ready.

scenes.goal: Go home and try to sleep

journal.t: If she'd loved me, I'd have fought the whole world. But there was nothing to fight for. That's what's so hard.
I'm done. I don't care who stays. If you want to leave, leave.
My hands keep shaking. My head is too loud. Maybe it isn't just heartbreak.

lines.t: A strange thing happens after the engagement notice. A few weeks of being wrecked, and then... quiet. Like a fever breaking.
The closure I'd waited ten years for finally came. Not the way I wanted. But it came. I could stop asking. I felt, for the first time in years, a little bit light.
I decided to stay single. To live my own life. No more complicated anything.
Back at the main office. Two to ten. And at the Port Ellis desk, finally in person after two years of dots and dashes: Viola Sutton.
Well, well. The relay hermit. You're taller than you tap.
How do I tap short?
You tap like a man who's saving his words for something. Sit, sit. Night desk gets supper at eight, you'll eat with us. I'll tell you everything you missed.
She does. She tells him everything. He listens. That's how it always was on the wire, and it's how it is in person.

choice.prompt: Viola is mid-story about the coal man.

say.t: See? You do have a laugh in there. I knew it.

opts.t: Ask her a question about herself.

say.t: About me? Nobody asks about me. ...Alright. Sit down. This'll take a while.

scenes.goal: Report back to the main wire office

lines.t: Every night at eight, the night desk eats together. Afterwards, everyone washes their tins at the basin in the back. It's the one time all day nobody's tapping.
One evening, at the basin, Viola reaches past him for the soap and ends up very close. Face to face. Close enough that neither of them moves for a second.
That night he walks her home down Willow Lane, like he usually does now.
At the basin, tonight. Did you feel that?
Feel what?
A spark. I felt a spark, Eli. Don't pretend you didn't notice.
He didn't expect it. Not this. Not from her.

choice.prompt: How do you answer?

opts.t: The truth: "Viola, I've always thought of you as... one of the boys. Somebody I'm easy around."

say.t: One of the boys. Wonderful. Every girl's dream.
Then think about it. I'll wait. Not forever, but I'll wait.
Say something, Eli. Anything.

lines.t: If you don't feel it too, then... I'll stop. Talking to you so much, I mean. It won't be fair on me otherwise.
She was already picturing us like a stage romance. Moonlight and violins. She saw love so differently from me. But she was the only person who'd talked to me every day for two years.

scenes.goal: Walk Viola home down Willow Lane

lines.t: She convinces him to try. Or he convinces himself. He's never been sure which.
But first he has to tell her who he is. All of it. He's never said it out loud, not in order, not to anyone.
I need you to know some things first. Before anything.

He tells her about the quiet house. Pa's three letters a year. The ruler. The coach stop and the two coins. The seventh year. The porch. The shaking hand that wasn't hers, or was. The telephone call. The engagement notice.
Halfway through, he realizes his face is wet. He didn't feel it start.
All those years I couldn't cry. And it came out at the end of a pier, in front of a girl I wasn't even sure I loved.
I'm not in a good place, Viola. I don't know if I can be what you want. I keep my distance from people. I don't know how not to.
...Then we'll go slowly. No promises. No... commitments. We'll just see. Can we just see?

choice.prompt: She's holding your hand.

opts.t: "Are you sure you want this? Want me?"

say.t: I'm sure. I've been sure since the relay shack.

lines.t: I knew she'd had a love before, a serious one. I knew she was used to boys falling over themselves for her. I wasn't like that. I didn't chase. But she wanted me anyway. And I hadn't been wanted in a very long time.

scenes.goal: Meet Viola at the east pier to talk properly

lines.t: They see each other every day. And almost from the start, they understand love completely differently.
She wants a note on his desk every morning. She wants him to ask, every day, if she's eaten. She wants to hear it, often, out loud, in the ways she's used to hearing it.
He believes two people should be free. That you shouldn't have to report every hour of your life. That someone's presence is the proof, not the routine.
You were talking to Nell. On the night desk. For twenty minutes.
She asked me how to fix her sounder.
For twenty minutes? It's a sounder, Eli, not a steam engine.
...I'll just. Go. Over there.

choice.prompt: Viola's eyes are wet.

say.t: You always say that. And then you forget to ask if I ate.

opts.t: "I'm allowed to talk to people, Viola."

say.t: I know you're allowed! I'm not stupid! I just want to feel like I'm the one you choose.

opts.t: "I need time. I've never done this. I'm learning."

say.t: ...I know. I know you are. I'm sorry. I just get frightened.

lines.t: I'm not alright. I think you should leave me alone tonight.
He goes. An hour later, a note under his door: "I won't ever leave you like that. Don't go. I didn't mean it."

It happened again. And again. I couldn't understand those turns. Leave me alone. Don't leave me. I needed time to learn her way of loving. And it felt like we were fighting every day over things I didn't understand.
Wanting reassurance isn't wrong. I know that. But needing room didn't mean I didn't care.

scenes.goal: Find out why Viola is upset with you

lines.t: The fair comes through, like it did when he was small. He takes Viola. The fire-eater. The sugar tent. A little painted boat bobbing at a rope.
I've been here before. When I was five. My aunt brought us. I've been looking for this exact spot my whole life.
And now you've found it. With me.
She's happy. Really happy, the uncomplicated way she's happy sometimes, like a child.
Early on, I'd told her I didn't think I'd ever marry. I didn't know what love was supposed to feel like. I'd been alone too long.
But somewhere along the way that changed. Standing on those planks, I could picture it. Her. A house. Ma liking her. A future, which I'd stopped believing in.

choice.prompt: Viola is leaning on the rail.

opts.t: "Viola... I think I'd marry you. If you'd have me. Someday."

say.t: Eli Ashby. Are you serious?
I'm always serious. It's my worst quality.
She cries and laughs at the same time. You make promises to each other on that pier. Real ones.
It's the best day.

lines.t: And if we ever part... don't worry about me. I'll be alright. I can take it.
He believes that when he says it.
On the way home, she squeezes his arm.
You take care of me like a husband would. Do you know that?
Nobody had ever said anything like that to me. I'd been alone so long. Those words went somewhere very deep, and stayed.

scenes.goal: Take Viola to the summer fair at the south pier

lines.t: Viola has a rheumatism of the joints. A real illness, a lifelong one. Some weeks her hands swell so badly she can't work the key.
Doc Whitlow gave her powders and rules. She doesn't always take the powders. She doesn't always follow the rules.
Did you take the powders today?
Don't. Don't be my doctor. Be my sweetheart.
I didn't want to treat her like a patient. I wanted her to live her own life. But I was frightened for her.

And there's something else. Something he knows, and has tried not to think about. She still has feelings for the man she loved before him. A man of a different faith. They'd both known it could never work. Knowing that didn't make the feelings go away.

choice.prompt: She's lying back on the pillows, eyes closed. You've wanted to ask for weeks.

opts.t: "Viola. Who do you want? Him, or me? I need to know."

say.t: ...I don't know. I don't want anyone. I don't want anything. I just want my hands to stop hurting.
She's ill. She's in pain. You know those words might not mean everything. But they go in like a nail.
I didn't ask. I'd changed my whole idea of my future to choose her. I couldn't bear to find out she wasn't choosing me the same way.

scenes.goal: Visit Viola. She's unwell again

journal.t: I love her. I think. Or I'm trying to, which might be the same thing.
I changed everything for her, and I don't know if she'd do the same.
I'm doing it all right and it still feels wrong. Something in me is going quiet again.

lines.t: It doesn't happen all at once. It happens the way a river changes course. Grain by grain.
The arguments. The expectations. The not-knowing. Slowly, what he feels for Viola stops being love and starts being something else. Care. Worry. Duty.
I still wanted her to be well. I still worried about her hands, about whether she'd eaten. I didn't want her to suffer. But the romantic part of me was going out like a lamp running dry.
Viola. I need some time. To... recover. I'm worn out. I'm not leaving. I just need room to breathe.
Room. From me.
From everything.
Then why can't it be like before? You used to walk me home every night. You used to look at me.

choice.prompt: She wants it back the way it was. You don't know how to give her that.

say.t: Try harder. Please.

opts.t: "It can't be like before. Not right now. I'm sorry."

say.t: Don't say that. Don't you say that to me.
You're doing it again. You're going away behind your eyes.

scenes.goal: Talk to Viola after your shift

lines.t: In the spring, the office takes on a new clerk for the ledger desk. Wren Ellery. Quiet hands. Ink on her cuff. She draws small birds in the ledger margins and erases them before Hargrove sees.
Mr. Hargrove says you know where everything is.
I know where everything was. Hargrove moves things to see if we notice.
Ha. So it's a test.
Everything's a test with Hargrove. Even the coffee.
He shows her the ledger. It takes an hour, and the hour goes very fast.

choice.prompt: She's looking at the margin where she drew a wren, half-erased.

opts.t: "You should leave that one. It's good."

say.t: It's a self-portrait. Wren. You see? Small and brown and judgmental.
I see a bird that's paying attention.
...That's a nice thing to say. You don't say many things, do you? But they're nice when you do.
Let him. Maybe he'll learn to appreciate the arts.
I saw that. Don't worry, I won't tell.

scenes.goal: Show the new clerk how the ledger works

lines.t: Their coaches leave from the same corner. They start walking there together. It happens without either of them deciding.
You go somewhere, sometimes. In the middle of a sentence. Like you've stepped out of the room for a minute.
...People usually don't notice that.
I notice things. It's my worst quality.
With Wren, he doesn't have to explain. He says half a thought and she finishes it. Not with what she wants it to mean. With what it means.

choice.prompt: Wren asks: "Where do you go?"

opts.t: Tell her the truth. "Somewhere quiet. Somewhere I don't have to be anyone."

say.t: That sounds lonely.
It is. But it's quiet.
Well. When you come back, I'll be here. Quietly. If that helps.
Alright. You don't have to tell me. But you can.
...That's alright too.

lines.t: I felt safe. I don't know a better word. With her, I felt safe. I didn't have to perform being a person. I could just be one.

scenes.goal: Walk to the coach with Wren

lines.t: You talk to her. Wren. You talk to her like you used to talk to me.
We walk to the coach. That's all.
You never tell me what you're thinking. Ever. And you tell her. I've seen your face when you talk to her. You don't make that face for me anymore.
She wasn't completely wrong. And that was the worst part.

But I wasn't looking for someone to replace her. I was looking for somewhere I could breathe. I'd been trying to tell her, for months, that we weren't working. She never heard it. Now it was all about Wren.
I loved her like a sister, Eli. Like my own sister. And now you—

choice.prompt: Viola is shaking.

opts.t: "This isn't about Wren. It's about us. We haven't been right for a long time."

say.t: Don't. Don't make it sound sensible. It's not sensible. I'm in pain.

opts.t: "I'm sorry. I'll stop walking with her."

say.t: I said it, and I felt something in me go dark, like a window being shuttered.

scenes.goal: Viola wants to talk

lines.t: Four o'clock. Coffee break. He walks to the Kettle & Lamp, like he does every Thursday.
Wren is there. She's come in from the other direction, from the bank. Neither of them planned it.
Oh! Hello. Fancy that.
Fancy that.
Well. I'm not drinking alone if you're standing right there. Sit.

choice.prompt: You sit down. It's just coffee.

opts.t: Talk about her birds, her family, anything.

say.t: She tells you about her grandmother, who kept canaries and named them all after presidents. You laugh. Really laugh.

opts.t: Tell her about your week. The real version.

say.t: She listens the way nobody's listened since Lettie Shaw. Not fixing. Just hearing.

opts.t: Drink your coffee and watch the street.

say.t: She doesn't fill the silence. She just drinks hers too. It's the most restful ten minutes you've had in a year.

lines.t: Outside the window, across the street, Viola is walking with Nell from the night desk.
Viola stops. She looks through the window. She sees them.
She doesn't come in. She doesn't wave. She turns around and walks the other way.
It was a coincidence. We hadn't planned it. We weren't hiding. We weren't trying to make anybody jealous. We were two people who happened to want coffee at four o'clock.
But I knew, the moment I saw her face, that it wouldn't matter what it was. Only what it looked like.

scenes.goal: Take your coffee break at the Kettle & Lamp

lines.t: Viola goes home and doesn't come back to work. She sends word through Nell: she's very ill. Her joints have flared. She can't get out of bed.
Then a package comes to the office, addressed to him. Inside is a Roentgen plate. An image of her hands, the bones grey and strange, the joints swollen.
Pinned to it is a note, in her handwriting.
Thank you for your gift.
Nell says Viola believes this might be the end. That it's his fault. That she was well until the coffee house.
I didn't know what to say. I couldn't breathe. "Thank you for your gift." Like I'd handed her the illness wrapped in paper.
He goes to Doc Whitlow. It's ten at night. Doc opens the door in his shirtsleeves.
Ashby. You look like you've seen a ghost. Come in. Sit.
Did I do this, Doc? To Viola. Did I make her sick?
I can't talk about my patients, son. You know that. But I can talk about illness in general, and I will.

Rheumatism of the joints is a disease of the body. It flares and quiets on its own schedule. Grief can make anybody feel worse, and stopping their medicine will certainly make them worse. But no man has ever given a woman that illness by drinking a cup of coffee.
You're not her disease. And you're not her cure.

choice.prompt: The words land somewhere you didn't know was waiting for them.

opts.t: "Then why do I feel like I'm both?"

say.t: Because somebody you care about told you that you were. And you believed her, because you're the kind of man who carries things. That doesn't make it true.
Get some sleep. You look worse than she does, and you're the one walking around.

opts.t: Stare at the plate in your hands.

say.t: Put that down, son. It's not yours to carry.

lines.t: I'm not a doctor. I couldn't cure her. I couldn't promise she'd be well if I stayed. And yet I felt like she believed I was the only one who could make her better.
Every time she said she needed me, I got angry. Not because I wanted her to suffer. Because I felt trapped inside a responsibility nobody could carry.

scenes.goal: Go to Doc Whitlow's. You need to understand

lines.t: At the office, the story is already written. Everybody knows Viola and Eli were sweet on each other. Everybody saw her get sick. Everybody heard about the coffee house.
The story is simple. Viola loved Eli. Eli was seen with Wren. Viola fell ill. Therefore.
I hope you're proud of yourself.
Ashby. A word. ...Keep your personal business out of my office. I won't have my operators falling to pieces over you.
Nobody knew my side. Nobody knew how long I'd been struggling before the coffee. How many times I'd said "I need time." The things she'd said that I still couldn't repeat.
They could all see her pain. Mine was private. I didn't have anybody to tell the whole story to.

choice.prompt: Hargrove is waiting.

say.t: I didn't want to make her a villain to save myself. She had her own fear and her own pain. But I didn't want to live inside a story where only hers counted.

opts.t: "Sir, there's more to it than what people are saying."

say.t: There always is. ...I'll take that under advisement. Get back to your key.
It's not much. But it's not nothing. He looks at you a little differently, after.

lines.t: Wren passes his desk with the ledger. She doesn't stop. She just leaves a small folded paper by his hand.
Inside: a drawing of a bird, sitting on a wire, in the rain. Underneath: "Still here. Quietly."

item.name: A bird on a wire, in the rain

scenes.goal: Go to work

lines.t: Viola is back on her feet. Thinner. Tired. Her hands wrapped in flannel. She lets him in.
He's tried to say it for months. Gently. Sideways. Hoping she'd hear it. Now he has to say it plainly.

I tried. I changed my mind about marriage for her. I tried to understand what she needed and explain what I couldn't give. I stayed after the feeling changed, because caring doesn't vanish just because things got hard.
But I can't keep being her partner without losing myself. And I've already lost so much of myself. There isn't much left to lose.
Say it. Whatever it is. I can see it in your face.

choice.prompt: This is the hardest thing you'll ever say. How do you end it?

opts.t: "I care about you. I always will. But I can't be your partner anymore. Not without disappearing. I'm sorry."

say.t: ...You said, if we ever parted, I shouldn't worry about you.
I did. I was wrong about that. But I meant the rest. I hope your hands get better. I hope you take the powders. I hope you find somebody who knows how to love you the way you need.
That's... that's a horrible, kind thing to say.
She cries. You let her. You don't leave until she tells you to. Then you leave.

opts.t: "I'll stay. I'll stay until you're well."

say.t: You will? You promise?
...I promise.
I said it, and something in me lay down and didn't get up.

opts.t: "We're done, Viola. I'm not your cure. Stop telling people I'm your disease."

say.t: Get out. Get out!
It was all true. It was also cruel. Both things walked out the door with you.
Eli? ...Eli, say something.
You don't. Nothing ends. Nothing gets better. It just goes quiet, the way things do when nobody is brave.

scenes.goal: Go to Viola's lodging. It's time to talk

journal.t: I can care about someone and still leave when it isn't healthy for me. Both are true.
I'm her disease and her cure. That's what everyone thinks. Maybe they're right.
I'm done being responsible for everyone's feelings. Starting now.

lines.t: He saddles Pilgrim. He opens the gate.
He's at the office. Pilgrim is tied at the rail. His coat is on the hook.
I don't remember the ride. I know I took it. I know every turn. But if you asked me to picture it, the bridge, the mill, the depot... there's nothing there. Just a blank where the road should be.
Like somebody else rode my horse and parked me at my desk.
It's happened before. It keeps happening. Home to work. Work to home. Whole hours, folded away somewhere he can't find them.
I'm not drinking. I sleep seven hours, more or less, in pieces. I'm not ill, that I know of. So what is this?
What if I'm on the road one day, and I'm not there, and somebody steps out in front of the horse?

choice.prompt: You sit at your key. Your hands are steady, for once. It's the rest of you that's far away.

opts.t: Press your palms flat on the desk. Feel the wood. Name five things you can see.

say.t: The key. The window. The inkwell. Hargrove's hat. Wren's bird in the ledger margin. ...Alright. I'm here. I'm here.

opts.t: Start working. Don't think about it.

scenes.goal: Ride to work

lines.t: At night it's two voices. They argue in him like two people in the next room.
You need someone. Someone to hold onto. Someone to tell you it's going to be alright. Find somebody. Anybody. Just don't be alone with this.
Leaning your whole weight on another person is how you ended up here. It didn't work with Viola. It won't work with anyone. Someone else can't carry you out of this.
Then who will?
...I don't know. You, maybe. Eventually.
I can't even feel my own hands.
Sometimes the disappointment turns into anger. And after the anger, something goes flat and far away, like a painted backdrop.

choice.prompt: Both voices are waiting for you to pick a side.

opts.t: "You're both right. I need people. I just can't make one person my whole floor."

say.t: ...That's actually sensible.
I hate it. But fine.

opts.t: Side with the one that wants comfort.

say.t: See? We'll find someone. It'll be fine.
That's what you said last time.

opts.t: Side with the one that wants to shut everything out.

say.t: That's not what I said. I said you'd have to learn to stand. Not that you'd have to stand alone forever.

opts.t: Let them argue until you fall asleep.

scenes.goal: Go home

lines.t: He wakes up. Ma's at the stove. Bacon. Coffee. Ordinary.
Morning, sleepyhead. You've got chalk on your face.
Chalk?
Wash up. The coach comes at half past eight. Old Amos won't wait.
Old Amos. Old Amos has been dead for six years.
He wakes up.
The room is dark. It's four in the morning. He's in his own bed. There's no bacon.
A dream. A dream of waking up. That keeps happening too. I wake up and it's not real, and I wake up again and I'm not sure.
He waits for the window to go grey. He gets up. He walks downstairs. Ma is at the stove.
You're up early. Couldn't sleep?

choice.prompt: Is this one real?

opts.t: Touch the doorframe. It's solid. Splintery. "This one's real."

say.t: What's real? Are you alright, son?
...Eli. Sit down. Sit down right now and tell me what's going on.
For the first time, you tell her. Not everything. But the dreams. The road. The hours you lose. She listens with both hands around her cup, very still.
Then you go see Doc Whitlow. This week. I'll go with you if you want. I'm not asking.
It's real. Probably. You eat without tasting it.

scenes.goal: Wake up

lines.t: You've been staring at that cup for ten minutes, Ashby. It's not going to tell your fortune.
You're gone again. Where are you?
Rook knows everything about him. More than anyone. And still not all of it. Nobody knows all of it. That's partly Eli's doing; it's always been easier to say "fine" and move on than to explain.
People say you look like you don't care. Like nothing touches you. But you've never been like that. You care so much it fries your wires.
Brother from another mother. Tell me what's going on.

choice.prompt: Your two oldest friends are waiting.

opts.t: Tell them everything. The road. The dreams. The voices.

say.t: ...How long has this been happening?
Since the engagement. Maybe before. I don't know. I can't tell where it started.
Right. Then we find out. Together. You don't get to do this one quietly.
Liar. You've been saying that since we were twelve. One day you'll tell me. I'll be here when you do.

opts.t: "I don't know how to explain it."

say.t: Then don't explain. Just say a piece of it. We'll put the rest together.

scenes.goal: Meet Rook at the Kettle & Lamp

lines.t: He goes. Ma comes with him and waits outside, pretending to read a seed catalog.
So. You, this time. Tell me.

choice.prompt: Doc Whitlow is listening.

opts.t: Tell him all of it. The lost hours, the dreams, the shaking, the voices, the feeling that you aren't real.

say.t: Alright. Thank you. That can't have been easy.

What you're describing, the feeling of being outside yourself, of the world being painted on glass... I've seen it before. In soldiers back from the war. In widows. In people who've carried too much for too long without setting it down.
It isn't madness, son. It's a mind that's been running hot for years, trying to protect you by pulling the curtains.
Will it stop?

It can. It often does. But not by itself, and not if you keep pushing through it like a mule through mud. There's a doctor in Port Ellis who works with the nerves. I'll write to him. You'll sleep, eat, walk. You'll talk to someone regularly. And you'll stop riding that horse when you're not all there.
...Alright.
"Alright." Ha. From you, I'll take that as a contract.

opts.t: Tell him only about the sleep.

say.t: Sleep powders, then. And come back if it's more than sleep. I suspect it is.

opts.crackNote: You open your mouth and the curtain comes down. "I'm fine, Doc."

say.t: Your mother's outside pretending to read about turnips. Want me to bring her in?

lines.t: Outside, Ma closes the seed catalog.
Well?

choice.prompt: Ma is holding your arm.

opts.t: "I'm going to be alright, Ma. Not today. But I'm going to be."

say.t: I know you are. You're careful. You get that from me.
Hm. Then we'll get you rested.

scenes.goal: See Doc Whitlow about yourself this time

journal.t: My feelings, memories and experiences deserve to be taken seriously. Including by me.
I'll push through. I always have.
I'm afraid this is just who I am now.

lines.t: Lately, whenever he plans to meet Wren after work, something gets in the way. Her sister visits. Hargrove keeps her late. The coach changes its time.
He starts to wonder. Whether she's pulling away. Whether he's been too much, without noticing.
Would you walk to the coach with me tonight?
Oh— not tonight. I'm sorry. My sister's in town again. She's... a lot. Another time?
"Another time." I've heard that before. From Delphine, on a note. It sounded exactly the same.
...Or maybe it doesn't. Maybe I'm reading every small change through ten years of bad weather.

choice.prompt: Wren is putting on her coat.

opts.t: "Of course. Another time. I hope your sister's visit is kind."

say.t: Kind? Ha. She'll reorganize my kitchen. ...Thank you, though. Really.
What? No. No, Eli. Truly. It's just my sister. I promise.
...Eli? I mean it. Another time.

scenes.goal: Ask Wren if she'd like to walk after work

lines.t: Ezra is fishing off the creek bridge, the way he has since they were nine. He's never caught anything.
If I see her, I want to ask her something. Before I say anything else.
Ask her what?
Whether she's comfortable. With how close I've been. Whether I'm too much. Expecting too much. I want her to be able to tell me the truth, even if it's bad.
And then?
If she says I'm too close, I listen. I step back. I don't make her responsible for how I feel.
If she says she's comfortable... then I'll tell her that I feel safe with her. And ask if there's room for me in her life. Not as a sweetheart. Not with any promise she has to keep. Just... close.
Ezra reels in his empty line.
Eli. That's the most grown-up thing I've ever heard you say.
In the seventh year you couldn't say four words to a girl on a wall. Look at you.

choice.prompt: Ezra is smiling.

say.t: Good. It means it matters. Be terrified and ask anyway.
Then she says no, and you're still a man who asked properly. That doesn't get taken away.

scenes.goal: Find Ezra at the creek bridge

lines.t: She sends a note on the Friday. "My sister's gone home. I've always wanted to see the view from that old tower you talk about. Sunday?"
So here they are. The top of the old water tower in Larkspur, where Rook first pointed out a yellow window on a hill, a lifetime ago.
The window's dark now. The Marlowes moved away years ago.
It's beautiful. You can see the whole valley. Is that your mother's house? With the lamp?
She lights it every night. Until I'm home.
That's the loveliest thing I've ever heard.
The sun is going down behind the mill. It's now or never. It's always been now or never. He's spent his whole life choosing never.

choice.prompt: What do you ask her?

opts.lock: You don't trust yourself to ask it plainly. Not yet.
opts.t: "Before I say anything... can I ask you something? Are you comfortable with how I've been around you? Have I been too close, or expected too much? I want the truth. Even if it hurts."
"Wren, I think I'm falling in love with you."

opts.crackNote: Your heart is going. The sun drops behind the mill.

opts.t: Look at the view. Say nothing.

lines.t: ...Eli. Nobody's ever asked me that. Not like that. Not first.
Yes. I'm comfortable. You've never once made me feel like I owe you anything. That's... rarer than you know.
Then can I tell you something? I feel safe with you. That's all. I don't need you to be anything. I just wanted to ask if there's room for me in your life. Close. However close you want.
There's room. There's a whole chair. ...I don't know what we are yet. But I'd like to find out slowly. Is slowly alright?
Slowly is the only speed I know.
...Thank you for asking that first. Really. Most people just say the big thing and leave you holding it.
Honestly? Sometimes it's been a little much. I care about you. I do. But I've got my own weather, and I need to go slow. Can we stay friends? Real ones. And see?
Yes. Of course. Thank you for telling me the truth.
...I'm glad you asked. Because, honestly, yes. It's been too close for me. I don't think I can be what you need, Eli. I need a little space.
Then you'll have it. Thank you for telling me. I mean that.
Oh. Oh, Eli. ...I don't know what I feel yet. You're so dear to me. But that's a big thing to hand someone on top of a tower.

lines.t: Give me time? Not a no. Just... time.

lines.t: Eli... I'm sorry. I don't feel that way. I care about you. But I don't. I'm so sorry.

lines.t: She means it kindly. It's the kindest no you've ever been given. It still lands like a stone.

lines.t: You look at the view. She looks at the view. The sun goes down. She says it's getting cold. You walk her back to the coach.
Another time. There's always another time. There's always the next pillar, the next coach, the next Sunday.
The lamps come on, one by one, across the whole of Larkspur. Ma's is the first.

scenes.goal: Meet Wren at the old water tower in Larkspur

journal.t: Whatever she said, I asked. I asked the right way. That's mine to keep.
I don't need anyone to choose me to be worth something. I'm learning that.
It doesn't matter. Nothing ever does.

present.title: Present Again
present.sub: You learned to care without losing yourself.

lines.t: The next October. The lamp in the window. The tin box on the kitchen table instead of under the bed.
Eli sees the nerve doctor in Port Ellis every second Thursday. Some weeks are good. Some weeks the curtain comes down, and he sits, and names five things, and waits for it to lift. It always lifts.
He rides to work and remembers the bridge. The mill. The hawk on the fence post. He's started noticing hawks.
Viola wrote, once, in the spring. Her hands are better. She's taking the powders. She's walking out with a schoolteacher who sends her a note every morning. Eli wrote back: "I'm so glad." He was.
And on Sundays, Wren comes to supper. Ma likes her. Ma pretends not to, which is how you know.
That girl draws birds on my napkins.
I know, Ma.
...Keep her.
Into the tin box, on top of everything else, goes a drawing of a bird on a wire. Not in the rain this time. In the sun.
I still care. I just learned how to do it without disappearing.
And for once, I'm giving myself the same patience I spent my whole life trying to give everyone else.

room.title: Room at the Table
room.sub: There was room for you after all.

lines.t: The next October. Wren comes to supper on Sundays, and they walk to the coach on Thursdays, and they take things slowly, the way he promised.
He still loses the road some mornings. He hasn't told anyone how often. One day he'll see someone about it. One day.
But there's a chair at the table with a bird drawn on the napkin beside it. And Ma's lamp is lit. And for now, that's a great deal.
I asked. She answered. I'm still here. For a long time I didn't think all three of those could be true at once.

kindno.title: Alone, Not Lonely
kindno.sub: She gave you the truth. You gave it back with grace.

lines.t: The next October. He and Wren still eat lunch together on Thursdays. Friends. Real ones. It's not what he hoped. It's something he didn't know he needed.
He fishes off the creek bridge with Ezra on Sundays. They never catch anything.
You alright?
Yeah. I am, actually. Not happy, exactly. But here.
Here's good. Here's a start.
Maybe moving on doesn't mean finding someone new. Maybe it just means being alone for a while, not as a punishment, but as a place to rest.

cure.title: The Cure
cure.sub: You stayed, and slowly stopped being anyone at all.

lines.t: He stays. Of course he stays. He brings the powders. He asks every morning if she's eaten. He walks her home every night.
Viola gets a little better, and then a little worse, and every time she's worse, he hears "thank you for your gift," even when she doesn't say it.
Years go by. He's very good at the wire. He's very good at being needed. He's no good at all at being himself; he's forgotten who that was.
Wren left the office the following spring. He never asked her anything.
I wanted to be someone's cure. I became someone's furniture.

stone.title: Stone
stone.sub: Nothing gets in now. Nothing gets out.

lines.t: He shuts every door. Viola. Wren. Rook, eventually, who keeps knocking for a year and then stops.
He goes to work. He comes home. Ma's lamp is lit. He turns it down himself now, so she won't wait up.
Nothing hurts. That was the idea. He just didn't know that nothing would also mean nothing.
I made myself into stone so no one could break me. It worked. It worked perfectly.

stone.retryLabel: Go back to the winter at the office

autopilot.title: Autopilot
autopilot.sub: The road keeps going. You just aren't on it.

lines.t: He rides to work. He rides home. He doesn't remember either. Pilgrim knows the way; Pilgrim has always known the way.
The tin box stays under the bed. He means to open it again someday. He doesn't remember to.
Ma's lamp is lit in the window every night. Some nights he sits in the yard and looks at it for an hour, and can't feel why it matters, only that it does.
I'm here. I think I'm here. If someone finds this, please. Ask me how I am. Ask me twice.

autopilot.retryLabel: Go back to the morning ride

unsaid.title: The Unsaid
unsaid.sub: Another time. There's always another time.

lines.t: Wren moves to Port Ellis in the spring. A better position, she writes. "Thank you for the tower. I'll never forget the view."
He keeps the bird drawing in the tin box, on top of the autograph page, on top of the letters, on top of the splinter of yellow wood.
A box full of things he never said.
Next time. Next time I'll ask.
...I've been saying that since the seventh year.
